messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Auditor
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 41

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed, Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark
  Maladaptive Strategies: Smoking: I smoke, Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous, Avoid Talking: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rangi Parata is a 46-year-old widowed Māori man who works as an auditor for a mid-sized accounting firm in Auckland, though he relocated to the Pacific Northwest of the United States several years ago following his wife's death. He presented for psychological assessment after his supervisor noted a marked deterioration in his work performance over the preceding eight months, and after a close colleague expressed concern that Rangi had become almost entirely unreachable outside of structured work hours.

Eighteen months ago, Rangi was visiting relatives on a small island community when a severe tropical cyclone made landfall with little warning. He had been staying in a low-lying coastal home with several family members when the storm surge came — not as a dramatic wave, but as a silent, relentless rise of dark water that crept under the doors and climbed the walls in the middle of the night. He described waking in complete darkness to the sound of nothing: an absence of the usual night insects, the ocean, any wind. That silence lasted perhaps forty seconds before the water reached the bed frame. By the time he and his relatives reached the roof, the water was at chest height inside the house. The smell of churned seawater, mud, and what he later understood was sewage from ruptured pipes saturated everything. At one point, in the darkness, he swallowed a mouthful of the floodwater. They remained on the roof for nearly six hours until rescue came at dawn. Two community members did not survive. Rangi was physically unharmed.

In the months that followed, the memory of that night returned to him not as a coherent story but as sensory fragments — the specific mineral-rot taste of the floodwater arriving without warning, the smell of disturbed sediment appearing when he opened a drain or walked past a river, so vivid and unbidden that he would stop mid-stride. He had come to believe that the memory was so extreme, so outside the range of anything that should happen to a person, that it sometimes felt as though it had happened to someone else entirely — a story he had read rather than lived. This unreality offered no comfort. If anything, it deepened his sense that something fundamental had broken in him.

He had come to feel that happiness itself was a warning sign. When he noticed himself relaxed — watching television, finishing a meal, sitting quietly on his porch — a cold alertness would move through him, a certainty that ease was the condition that preceded catastrophe. He had stopped allowing himself to settle. He smoked steadily throughout the day, a habit that had resumed after fifteen years of abstinence. At work, where he spent long hours reviewing financial records in a quiet open-plan office, unusual silences between colleagues made him look up and scan the room. When a report took longer to load than expected, or when a colleague didn't respond to an email within what he considered a reasonable window, he found himself certain that something had gone wrong — not with the computer or the schedule, but in the world outside. He had declined every invitation to visit new client sites, telling his supervisor he preferred to work remotely, because he was certain that unfamiliar buildings and streets offered dangers he could not yet see or calculate.

He had not spoken to any of his relatives about the cyclone or its aftermath, and he deflected whenever friends raised it. He had stopped visiting the waterfront neighbourhood where he initially lived after relocating, and he kept his apartment curtains drawn after dark. Waking in the night to a dark room would bring the floodwater back so completely — taste, smell, the weightless terror — that he would sit on the edge of his bed until morning.

What Rangi expressed most quietly, almost as an aside, was that he felt dead inside — that the grief and the fear had not so much overwhelmed him as hollowed him out. He was certain that bad things would continue to find him regardless of what he did. He came to therapy not because he believed it would help, but because his supervisor had made it a condition of continued employment, and because, as he put it, he had nothing left to lose by trying.
